function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve data. This function is commonly used for API calls and web scraping. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The Date Nager API provides access holiday information for over 100 countries, including the ability to query for long weekends. It leverages ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country codes to tailor the search to your specific region of interest. More information can be found in https://date.nager.at/Api

headers.description: Optional headers to send with the request as a dictionary of header values.

Content-Type.description: The media type of the resource being requested, typically 'application/json'.

Authorization.description: The credentials to authenticate a user agent with a server, typically formatted as 'Bearer {token}'.

timeout.description: The maximum amount of time to wait for a response from the server, in seconds. A longer timeout may be necessary for slower network connections or overloaded servers. This is a float type value.

params.description: URL parameters to append to the URL. Sent as a dictionary of key-value pairs.

query.description: The query parameter for search or filtering.

page.description: The page number parameter for pagination. Used to retrieve a specific page of results.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials formatted as a tuple of strings (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem), if required for the request.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names and values.

sessionid.description: Session identifier cookie, used to recognize client sessions on the server.

csrftoken.description: CSRF protection token cookie, used to prevent cross-site request forgery attacks.

proxies.description: Proxy settings as a dictionary, mapping protocol or protocol and hostname to the URL of the proxy.

http.description: Proxy URL to use for HTTP requests, including the port number.

https.description: Proxy URL to use for HTTPS requests, including the port number.

stream.description: Whether to stream the download of the response. If False, the response content will be immediately downloaded. Streaming is useful for handling large files or responses.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not. Set to False to skip certificate verification, which is not recommended unless you are sure of the server's identity.

Here’s a quick play‑by‑play guide to finding a 2‑hour‑or‑shorter movie that’s within walking distance of Times Square (roughly a 10–15‑minute walk, ~0.5 mi). | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **1. Pick a theater** | • **AMC Empire 25** – 25 screens, 2‑hour‑plus blockbusters plus indie titles.
• **Regal Times Square** – 12 screens, often shows independent & art‑house films.
• **Film Forum** (Broadway & 42nd St.) – 4‑screen arthouse venue, great for shorter films.
• **IFC Center** (Broadway & 45th St.) – 4‑screen arthouse, known for indie releases.
• **Theater at the Brooklyn Academy of Music (BAM)** – a bit farther (~1 mi), but worth it for curated short‑form cinema. | All are within a 10–15‑minute walk from Times Square. | | **2. Check the showtimes** | • Go to the theater’s official site (e.g., ) or use a ticket‑booking platform like **Fandango** or **AMC’s app**.
• Look for the “Showtimes” tab and pick the date you’re interested in. | These sites list every screening, including start times and durations. | | **3. Filter by runtime** | • On most sites you’ll see the runtime next to each film (e.g., “The Grand Budapest Hotel – 1h 39m”).
• If the site doesn’t show runtime, you can quickly look up the film on **IMDb** or **TMDb** (search the title → “Runtime” field).
• Keep an eye out for films that are **≤ 120 minutes**. | This ensures you won’t be stuck in a marathon. | | **4. Pick a film that fits** | Here are a few examples that *often* run under 2 hours and are likely to be in the lineup (check the current schedule to confirm):
• **“The Grand Budapest Hotel”** – 1h 39m (if still showing).
• **“Moonrise Kingdom”** – 1h 58m.
• **“Lady Bird”** – 1h 44m.
• **“The Farewell”** – 1h 48m.
• **“The Lighthouse”** – 1h 57m.
• **“The Big Sick”** – 1h 52m.
• **“The Peanut Butter Falcon”** – 1h 46m.
• **“The Last Black Man in San Francisco”** – 1h 56m.
• **“The Florida Project”** – 1h 47m.
• **“The Shape of Water”** – 1h 59m. | These are all under 2 hours and are frequently screened at the theaters listed above. | | **5. Buy tickets** | • Once you’ve chosen a film, click “Buy Tickets” on the theater’s site or on Fandango.
• Select the screen, seat, and payment method.
• You’ll receive a confirmation email or QR code to scan at the theater. | Saves you a trip to the box office and guarantees a seat. | | **6. Arrive early** | • Aim to arrive at least 10–15 minutes before the start time to find your seat and settle in. | Keeps you on schedule and lets you enjoy the film without rushing. | ### Quick “One‑Stop” Option If you want to avoid hunting through multiple sites, try **Fandango**: 1. Visit . 2. In the search bar, type “Times Square, NY” and hit **Enter**. 3. The map will show all nearby theaters. Click on one (e.g., AMC Empire 25). 4. Browse the list of films; runtimes are shown next to each title. 5. Click “Buy Tickets” for the film you like. ### Bonus: Use Google Maps for Walking Distance - Open Google Maps. - Search “AMC Empire 25” or “Regal Times Square.” - Click “Directions” → “Walking.” - The route will show the exact walking time (usually 10–15 min). --- #### Final Tip Because film lineups change daily, it’s best to check the theater’s website or a ticket‑booking platform on the day you plan to go. That way you’ll know exactly which films are playing, their runtimes, and whether they’re still under 2 hours. Enjoy your movie night!
